title: Fulvio Lucisano, Italian Producer of ‘Planet of the Vampires’ and ‘What Have You Done to Solange?,’  Dies at 98
description: Italian producer Fulvio Lucisano, who shepherded a slew of cult B-movies such as “Planet of the Vampires” and “What Have You Done to Solange?” and h
body:
Italian producer Fulvio Lucisano, who shepherded a slew of cult B-movies such as “Planet of the Vampires” and “What Have You Done to Solange?” and had a close rapport with Roger Corman, has died. He was 98.

	His daughter Paola confirmed Lucisano’s death on Tuesday in a statement sent to Italian news agency ANSA, writing: “Rest in peace, Dad.”

	Over seven decades in the film business, Lucisano mounted more than 150 projects in a panoply of genres, ranging from Mario Bava’s pulpy classic “Planet of the Vampires” to Franco Zeffirelli’s “The Young Toscanini,” starring Elizabeth Taylor as a primadonna soprano, as well as Buster Keaton-starrer “War, Italian Style.”
	

	Lucisano’s genre purview included sci-fi, horror, Italian comedies and soft porn, but also highbrow works by some of Italy’s most revered auteurs like Liliana Cavani, Marco Ferreri, Lina Wertmuller and European arthouse greats like Carlos Saura, whose 1999 work “Goya in Bordeaux” Lucisano was particularly proud of.


	“Genres don’t exist,” Lucisano said in a 2008 interview with Variety. “The only thing I care about is the moviegoers. They are our judge.”

	In the interview, Lucisano said he had always paid heed to the advice Keaton gave him in 1966 on the Rome set of “War, Italian Style,” in which Keaton played a hapless German general, one of his last roles.

	“He told me: ‘Any kind of movie you make, look at what happens in the first reel, and make sure that, if it’s a comedy, there’s a laugh early on; if it’s a drama or an action movie, then something surprising has to happen in the first 10 minutes,'” Lucisano said.
	

	The Rome-born Lucisano started out in production in 1949, assisting an American company making a Catholic documentary shot inside the Vatican and St. Peter’s to commemorate the coming year’s Holy Year Jubilee. A lawyer’s son who had a degree in law himself, Lucisano personally drafted his own contracts for most of his career.

	He set up Italian Intl. Film (IIF) in 1958 and soon started collaborating with Los Angeles-based American Intl. Pictures, James H. Nicholson and Samuel Z. Arkoff’s low-budget Hollywood studio that spawned Corman’s films, which were distributed in Italy by Lucisano’s Italian Intl. Film.

	Their collaboration started with 1962’s “Warriors Five,” a WWII drama starring Jack Palance; followed by “Sexy magico,” a faux docu about sexual rites around the world; and in 1964 came campy Jane Mansfield-starrer “Primitive Love,” a mondo sex farce in a similar vein.

	in 1965, Lucisano proudly shepherded Bava’s “Planet of the Vampires,” his first picture shot in Cinecitta’s legendary Studio 5, later to become Federico Fellini’s second home. “Planet of the Vampires,” considered a major influence on Ridley Scott’s “Alien,” was a co-production with American Intl. Pictures.

	“What Have You Done to Solange?” is one of Lucisano’s relatively early productions that he liked to reminisce about. It’s a now-classic 1972 England-set giallo and a favorite of Quentin Tarantino, helmed by Massimo Dallamano with a typically atmospheric Ennio Morricone score.

	In 2005, the Venice Film Festival celebrated Lucisano with a special Fulvio Lucisano Day as part of its Tarantino-presented “Secret History of Italian Cinema” retrospective, during which restored copies of both “Vampires” and “Solange” screened.

	But besides Italian B-movies, Lucisano also shepherded a slew of artier titles.

	In 1975, just three years after “Solange,” Lucisano made Mauro Bolognini’s “Per le antiche scale” (“Down the Ancient Staircase”), a dark drama starring Marcello Mastroianni as a psychologist trying to isolate an “insanity virus” in a Fascist-era asylum. It won the Locarno Film Festival’s Special Jury nod.

	He produced Liliana Cavani’s Nazi-era “The Berlin Affair,” Luigi Comencini’s “A Boy From Calabria” and Francesca Archibugi’s 1993 foreign-language Oscar-nommed debut “Il grande cocomero” (“The Great Pumpkin”), just to name a few of his forays into auteur territory.
	

	As a distributor, IIF has released hundreds of pics, including “Thelma and Louise,” thanks to a strong relationship he had with MGM; Andrei Konchalowski’s “Maria’s Lovers,” as part of a longstanding deal in those days with Menahem Golan’s Cannon; and “Four Weddings and a Funeral” through his tie at the time with Polygram. 

	Lucisano served as president of Italy’s motion picture association ANICA from 1998 to 2001.

	During his illustrious career, Lucisano was honored with five David di Donatello awards, including a lifetime achievement honor in 2009, as well as four Nastri d’Argento Silver Ribbon awards.

	Lucisano is survived by his daughters, Federica and Paola, who run his now publicly traded company called Lucisano Media Group.

schema.headline: Fulvio Lucisano, Italian Producer of ‘Planet of the Vampires’ and ‘What Have You Done to Solange?,’  Dies at 98

title: New Marilyn Monroe Barbie Doll Inspired by ‘Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend’ Ensemble
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Marilyn M
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Marilyn Monroe‘s birthday celebrations haven’t concluded quite yet. 

	Mattel is honoring the Hollywood icon with a new Barbie Signature doll inspired by her performance of “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend” in the 1953 musical “Gentlemen Prefer Blondes.” The collectible arrives Aug. 18, a little more than two months after what would have been Monroe’s 100th birthday on June 1. Monroe’s centennial has been marked throughout 2026 with exhibitions, auctions and other tributes to the actress, whose industry-spanning influence has endured more than six decades after her death.


		

			
			
	

	
					
		

										NEW RELEASE						

					Marilyn Monroe Barbie Signature Doll		

		
	

	The $81 doll recreates one of Monroe’s most recognizable screen looks: the hot-pink gown she wore while singing “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend,” complete with an oversized bow, dramatic opera gloves and sparkling jewelry. 

	“Barbie has a rich history of celebrating Marilyn Monroe’s legendary style as both a fashion icon and beloved actress,” Robert Best, Mattel’s vice president and dolls design creative director, said in a statement. Best added that the company wanted the doll to recognize Monroe not only for the famous pink gown, but also as “a savvy producer, a businesswoman and a boundary-breaking artist.”

	The new release continues a long history between Monroe and Barbie. Mattel previously created dolls based on several of her signature costumes, including the billowing white halter dress from “The Seven Year Itch,” a red sequined gown from “Gentlemen Prefer Blondes” and her one-shouldered evening gown from “How to Marry a Millionaire.” The company’s Monroe dolls date back to at least 1997.


	The Marilyn Monroe Barbie Signature Doll goes on sale Aug. 18 on Amazon for $81.

schema.headline: New Marilyn Monroe Barbie Doll Inspired by ‘Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend’ Ensemble

title: Stella Lefty on the Rise of ‘Boston’ and Her Sudden Fame: ‘When I First Started Writing Songs, No One Cared!’
description: Early this month, when the top 5 of the Billboard Hot 100 was occupied entirely by country artists for the first time in its history, most of the na
body:
Early this month, when the top 5 of the Billboard Hot 100 was occupied entirely by country artists for the first time in its history, most of the names were familiar: There was Taylor Swift, there was Ella Langley, there was Morgan Wallen, there was Morgan Wallen with Ella Langley… and at No. 5, 23-year-old newcomer Stella Lefty.

	If the Chicago-area native’s name doesn’t ring a bell, it’s a safe bet the song in question, “Boston,” does. Recently included in Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood “Up Next” class, Lefty is in the midst of a whirlwind year and has seen a sharp rise in streaming numbers following several viral songs on TikTok. Last week, she took a trip home to play Lollapalooza, announced her debut album “Long Way Home” (which comes out on Friday), and shared just how much life has changed for her, seemingly overnight.
	

	“There was this period where I moved to L.A. where I was grinding, and nothing was happening, which, you know, happens,” she told Variety backstage at Lollapalooza. “Every video I’d post would get, like, fucking one view, so I think it’s crazy to see what happened from those TikToks and how this has all played out. It’s also just so refreshing for me because I feel like I was getting so bogged down by where I was at before. I feel like I’ve circled around in terms of the sound and where everything is at, to a place that I feel really good about.”


	She began publicly sharing her songs in 2020 as the pandemic set in. Her goal was less of a marketing strategy and more of a need for an outlet. “When I write something that I love, I just want to put it out into the world,” she explains. But as the songs began to gain an audience, word spread that her father, Eric Lefkofsky, is a co-founder of Groupon and later founded Tempus AI, where he currently sits as CEO. Inevitably, the term “nepo baby” was thrown around. Rather than address it, Lefty has opted to keep her head down and focus on her music.
	

	She does, however, bring up the juxtaposition between the start of her career and now.

	“When I started writing songs, nobody was telling me what they thought. I was just in my room, so who was going to tell me that they thought my song was bad? No one cared! But when I moved to L.A., so many new opinions started coming in.” True to the album title, her motivation throughout the creative process was “trying to get back to a place where it all began, where I was writing in my room, whatever it was going to be and not overthinking it.”

	Still, the success of “Boston” means her options have expanded far beyond her bedroom. Asked about her dream collaborations, “Every day this changes for me,” she says with a laugh. “I love Hozier, so doing something with him would be epic. Obviously Taylor [Swift] and Miley [Cyrus] — I would probably die and never be able to speak again. Chris Stapleton, Gracie Abrams…” she concludes, “I’m a fan, you know?”

schema.headline: Stella Lefty on the Rise of ‘Boston’ and Her Sudden Fame: ‘When I First Started Writing Songs, No One Cared!’

title: SXSW Sets Podcast Festival, Locals-Only Perks and Changes in Music Venues for 2027 Event in Austin
description: South by Southwest has unveiled plans for a podcast festival, new locals-only perks and temporary changes in music venues for the 2027 event that wi
body:
South by Southwest has unveiled plans for a podcast festival, new locals-only perks and temporary changes in music venues for the 2027 event that will unfold on the streets of Austin, Texas in March.

	SXSW will run from March 15-21. The inaugural Podcast Festival will be held March 17-20. Open to all SXSW badgeholders, the podcast fest will feature live tapings and industry conversations. And the SXSW EDU conference for educators will be held once again just before the main event from March 13-16.
	

	SXSW has made changes in part because of the temporary shakeup in venues in Austin. The festival’s longtime home of the Austin Convention Center is under top-to-bottom renovation, while the stately Paramount Theatre on Congress Avenue main drag also will be out of commission next year for a restoration effort.


	In 2026, SXSW was reorganized as a seven-day event that sought to integrate the various strands — film, music, TV, digital and lifestyle — into a central area of downtown Austin.

	“2026 proved that we can evolve the event while preserving the discovery, connection and creativity that make it special,” said Greg Rosenbaum, SXSW’s senior VP of programming. “For 2027, we’re building on what worked by creating more intentional hubs across downtown Austin, giving growing communities like podcasting a bigger platform, and making it easier for attendees to find the ideas, people and opportunities that matter to them.”

	The festival’s Music Clubhouse will relocate to The Thompson hotel, with Music Conference programming more central to the event footprint at The Thompson and The Westin hotels. With the Paramount closed, some film premieres will be held at ACL Live at the Moody Theater, which accommodates about 2,800. The Film & TV Conference hub will be relocated to the Driskill and Stephen F. Austin hotels.
	

	This year, SXSW is introducing the CxO Badge for C-suite executives and the 512 Club to provide perks and access to local residents. Badgeholders with an Austin zip code will receive special perks leading up to the festival launch and the 512 Club will become a new downtown home base for residents at the festival.

	(Pictured: Charlotte Weinman of Horsepower performs at SXSW on March 17, 2026)

schema.headline: SXSW Sets Podcast Festival, Locals-Only Perks and Changes in Music Venues for 2027 Event in Austin

title: Ascend Literary Management Signs ‘Average Joe’ Creator Robb Cullen (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Ascend Literary Management has signed Robb Cullen for representation, Variety has learned exclusively. Cullen continues to be repped by IAG and Jare
body:
Ascend Literary Management has signed Robb Cullen for representation, Variety has learned exclusively. Cullen continues to be repped by IAG and Jared Levine, Sabrina Padwa and Jonathan Leiter of Yorn Levine.

	Cullen most recently created the series “Average Joe.” The series originally launched on BET+ in 2023, while the second season will debut on Paramount+ on Aug. 19. Deon Cole leads the cast of the series, which follows plumber Joe Washington (Cole) after he learns that his deceased father stole millions from the Russian mafia. Cullen is also an executive producer on the show. 
	

	In addition to “Average Joe,” Cullen co-created the FX series “Lucky,” which starred John Corbett. Cullen and his brother, Mark, received an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series for their work on the show’s pilot, which was directed by the Russo brothers of Marvel fame. 


	Cullen’s other TV credit include the Spike TV animated series “Gary the Rat,” and “Heis,” “Mr. Robinson,” and “Las Vegas” for NBC. He also co-wrote films like “Once Upon a Time in Venice” and “Cop Out,” both of which starred Bruce Willis. Cullen is currently developing projects for McG and Wonderland on a yet-to-be titled action drama. 

	Ascend was founded earlier this year by Ian Greenstein. Greenstein was previously at Innovative Artists Entertainment and before that spent over a decade at Gersh, where he led the agency’s TV department. He also spent over 10 years at Paradigm after the agency merged with Genesis, the boutique literary firm Greenstein co-founded in 2000.

schema.headline: Ascend Literary Management Signs ‘Average Joe’ Creator Robb Cullen (EXCLUSIVE)

title: North Korea-Focused Film Fund Bearing North Launches With ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A new private grantmaking initiative dedicated to films about North Korea has launched out of Los Angeles, with an advisory board drawn from documen
body:
A new private grantmaking initiative dedicated to films about North Korea has launched out of Los Angeles, with an advisory board drawn from documentary filmmaking, journalism, and human rights advocacy.

	Bearing North, founded by entrepreneurs and film investors Blaine Vess and Esther Paik Vess, will award grants to independent filmmakers worldwide at any stage of production. The initiative covers documentary features, narrative features, and short films, with a stated preference for projects brought forward by North Korean defectors.
	

	The founders bring prior involvement in the space: Blaine Vess has served on the board of Liberty in North Korea for more than a decade, and the couple have previously supported North Korea-related documentaries including “I Am Sun Mu,” “Assassins,” and “Beyond Utopia.”


	“Some of the films that have most shaped how we understand history arrived decades after the events they depict,” Blaine Vess said. “We created Bearing North because important stories about North Korea are unfolding now, while the people who lived them, the places where they happened, and the perspectives surrounding them are still within reach.”

	The initiative’s advisory group includes Matt Tyrnauer, director of “Valentino: The Last Emperor” and “Where’s My Roy Cohn?”; Anna Fifield, journalist and author of “The Great Successor”; Joseph Kim, North Korean defector and author of “Under the Same Sky”; Hannah Song, CEO of Liberty in North Korea; and Sokeel Park, chief strategy officer of Liberty in North Korea.

	Bearing North’s first supported project is “School for Defectors,” directed by Jeremy Workman. The documentary tracks students at the Jangdaehyun School in Busan, South Korea – an institution serving North Korean defectors and their families.
	

	“North Korea is often reduced to headlines about missiles and politics,” Blaine Vess said. “Great filmmakers have the ability to show us something much harder to capture: how ordinary people live, hope, adapt, and endure.”

	Grant applications are now open.

schema.headline: North Korea-Focused Film Fund Bearing North Launches With ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Angélique Kidjo Talks ‘Hope,’ Her Mother’s Legacy and Making History With a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame
description: Two things have been crucial to a restless Angélique Kidjo since her childhood in Benin, West Africa: diverse, universal, nuanced brands of truthful
body:
Two things have been crucial to a restless Angélique Kidjo since her childhood in Benin, West Africa: diverse, universal, nuanced brands of truthful musical storytelling in all its forms, and her mother.Selling nearly four million albums worldwide, winning five Grammys, writing a bestselling autobiography, “Spirit Rising,” with its foreword by Desmond Tutu, and becoming the first Black African artist to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame are all just icing on a very sweet cake. “This is everything to me,” she says loudly with a laugh (via Zoom) of her music, her mission and her mother, as she gesticulates wildly for punctuation at every turn. 

	She’ll receive her star Aug. 18 at 11:30 in a ceremony at  7011 Hollywood Blvd. Audiennces can watch on walkoffame.com.Since the start of her reign as a queen of West African music (this journalist first spoke to Kidjo in 1991 when “Logozo,” her debut album in the U.S., was released), or now, with 2026’s “Hope,” the singer-composer has been sure to acknowledge the ongoing influence of her mom — a choreographer and theater director — with zeal.As for the universality of her hypnotic, soulful sound and her dynamic, jazzy mezzo-soprano voice, Kidjo’s singing in five languages (Fon, French, Yorùbá, Gen-Mina and English) has forever been key to the funk, its frankness and her grace.Discussing “Hope’s” tour through 2027, “the stretching of my own physical boundaries” and playing music in a world that, though troubled, “may be better off and more unified than we think,” an energetic Kidjo talked about the need for reinvention.“How do I keep my mental health, my priorities and my values in check, and still be the person that I want to be, but evolving in this ever-changing ecosystem?” Kidjo wonders.But inventing herself in the first place is what leads listeners to every magical Kidjo milestone: 1996’s “Fifa” where she first sang in English; 2007’s “Djin Djin,” for which she won her first contemporary world music album Grammy; her back-to-back 2019 albums, “Remain in Light” and “Celia,” where she imaginatively captured the music of Talking Heads (“When I met David Byrne, I asked if he’s sure he’s American as he’d been speaking about my culture like he lived there forever,” she says) and Celia Cruz.Her new Africana-laced R&B album, “Hope,” with Pharrell Williams and Nile Rodgers, takes Kidjo to sleek pop places she’s rarely visited while maintaining her earthen, conscious lyricism. Then there are the works with minimalist classical composer Philip Glass on the poetic “Ife”: “Three Yoruba Songs” and “Symphony No. 12” (which additionally paid tribute to David Bowie’s “Lodger”) that Kidjo called “my greatest aesthetic challenges.”If she goes back to the start of her career, then before that to her childhood on stage at her mother’s Theatre du Benet company at age 6, Kidjo admits that “my values are the same values as always. They’re about me telling a compelling story, my compelling story… humanity stories,” all filled with the core values passed down to Kidjo by her parents.“Don’t come up with funny excuses,” she says. “When you do something wrong, you stand for it. If you deserve respect, give respect back. And if you deserve to be loved, you have to start loving yourself to be able to see the other person important to you. … My mom made me this person that I am by making me think about how my words can hurt. Mom always used to say a word is like an egg. When it falls, you can’t put it back. When you hurt somebody with your words, it stays. It’s pain. The pain you inflict on somebody’s soul with words has consequences for you too. Because when you put that bad stuff in the universe, it comes back changed. You might not like that change, and you don’t choose the time when it comes back.”Thinking about such consequences while living and thriving among her family (seven boys, three girls) during childhood, Kidjo was blessed with being loved and seen and given the opportunity and the freedom to speak freely and be herself.Those elements are the very core of her lifelong values, aesthetically, spiritually and humanistically.“I have been told by my uncles and aunties in the village that I was that child that always asked all the questions and never got enough answers,” Kidjo says, laughing.It’s important to note that as much gravitas and import that Kidjo placed upon her mother’s words and questions, there was a playful life lesson to be had between mother and daughter. Like having her mom, until the time of her passing during COVID-19, pushing Angélique to eat, nagging her to gain weight.“She told me that I needed to eat hamburgers in America, or to come home so that she could put some flesh on my bones,” Kidjo remembers.Earlier in their relationship, there was the back-and-forth between mother and child when it came to 6-year-old Kidjo demanding to play lead roles in her mother’s plays (“Why can’t I be the little girl that’s singing and doing all these things? I knew all the stuff by heart”), to being frightened when that same lead princess suddenly contracted malaria, and young Angélique had to go on.“Mom grabbed my ankle and I said, ‘Nah, I ain’t going on.’ Until she then put the costume on me and shot me on stage. I was just shaking like crazy. But I said to myself, ‘The heck with it. Just go for it.’ So, I start singing. Then I did all the crazy stuff that I do. Move around. Singing and playing the part. Then I finished, walked back, and suddenly, ovation. And my mom said, ‘You gotta go back.’”Young Angélique went back.But the child Kidjo turned into the teenage Kidjo, seeing success on national radio singing Miriam Makeba songs. That same teen sensation left West Africa due to troubles from its dictatorship, and moved to Paris under cover of night and a clandestine air flight. Once in Paris, Kidjo picked up where she left off, playing packed pop and jazz clubs and making African-French recordings until signing with Island and becoming an international sensation — all of which is reminiscent (save for secret night flights) of the trajectory of a Taylor Swift or a Sabrina Carpenter.What did it mean for Kidjo, then and now, to be a young woman growing up in the public eye in pop music?“You have to be aware,” she insists. “You have to be strong. You have to remind yourself that there’s always gonna be somebody that’s gonna say something nasty about you, gonna drag you into the mud. You can’t allow that. … You also can’t be the person who wants somebody to feel miserable for us to feel better. My mom said to me all the time, ‘Don’t be that. Don’t be that miserable person.’”Kidjo quickly told a tale about being a successful 12-year-old star, and coming back from school one afternoon with a crowd of people popping out of nowhere.“Boys and girls were spitting on me, calling me prostitute,” Kidjo says. “When I told my grandmother and my mother, they cleaned me up, and said ‘Do not let anyone define who you wanna be.’ You were talking about the ‘Logozo’ album right? I can remember, then, how the stylist who was hired told the record company, ‘Why are you calling a stylist to style an African girl? Don’t they walk naked in their countries?’ And, I was like, ‘Really? Let me show you what modernism looks like in my country.’ And I went out and bought that catsuit that is on the album cover — beautiful, no? I was fearless. No one could stop me.”Does she still have that iconic zebra-print catsuit from “Logozo’s” cover?“Oh yeah, I do. My daughter wore it for Halloween once.”Mothers and daughters and their bonds: their impact and import will never cease for Kidjo. There’s a reason her nickname is “Mama Africa.”Her “Eve” album of 2014 is dedicated to women, young and old, of her homeland. The Afrobeat-driven “Mother Nature” from 2021 is ripe with the vision of gentle feminine wisdom while 2019’s “Celia” sings praises to Cuba’s queen of salsa. And on the tracks “Aye Kan” and “No Stopping Us,” on “Hope,” the spirit of Kidjo’s mother lives on in her words and image.“In mourning, I was in shambles because I never thought that my mom gonna leave us so quickly,” Kidjo says quietly. “The day before she died, we had a wonderful conversation. Talking about music, about songs, this rhythm for that part. My mom was always looking for music all around the world, singing so many different songs to me, always giving me stuff to think about when it comes to music. If I was in front of this rhythm, what will I do? My mom was that person. She was still saying how people commented on how she don’t feed that kid, I’m so skinny. As we finished the conversation, she said, ‘Before you put me in the grave, you gotta sing my life after me. Make me that promise.’ And I’m telling her, ‘I’m not sure I’m gonna keep that promise. In my grief, I might not be able to.’ Now, remember, I’m taught that before you promise something, think about the commitment that you’re about to take. If you can’t do it, say no,” she says. “So, as I’m mourning, this is what I’m thinking to myself: How can I make the world discover her principles, those values that my mother gave all of us, even as we’re living in different parts of the world, being who we are?”Kidjo’s response to keeping that promise shines through — effortlessly, sonorously — on the 21st century African diasporic R&B of “Hope,” songs of empowerment against authoritarianism such as “Bando,” and lyrics dedicated to “opening each other’s eyes, that’s the mission.”“Hope was my mom’s favorite word; she used to say, ‘Your day starts with hope, your life starts with hope.’ Without hope, there’s nothing.”Making that promise another element of her responsibility to herself and to the world comes through in Kidjo’s consideration of becoming the first Black African artist to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.“For me, it is still like I’m in a dream. But you know what? My parents always used to say, ‘You have to dream big. Otherwise, shut up, don’t talk about it.’ So, for me, this is a door being open, on American soil, to welcome in artists from around the globe. And I am the first Black African to have this honor. For me, it becomes a responsibility. How do we sustain this and get the people that give me this honor to understand that I’m just the first one, that the door must stay open for all the trailblazers in Africa, Latin America, Europe, wherever in the world that should be there. Let’s keep that door open. Let’s remind ourselves that when we have something and we share it, that we have more to give.”Angélique Kidjo’s mother would be proud.

schema.headline: Angélique Kidjo Talks ‘Hope,’ Her Mother’s Legacy and Making History With a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame

title: C+C Music Factory Co-Founder Robert Clivillés Sues Freedom Williams for $30 Million, Alleging He Wrongfully Claimed Trademark Despite Never Being a Group Member
description: Whatever fallout came as a result of the canceled Freedom 250 concerts on the National Mall in Washington this summer, we can add a lawsuit that oth
body:
Whatever fallout came as a result of the canceled Freedom 250 concerts on the National Mall in Washington this summer, we can add a lawsuit that otherwise might not have happened. One prominent figure in that D.C. controversy, Freedom Williams, who made newsmaking statements in his role as frontman for the touring edition of C+C Music Factory, has been sued by the act’s surviving co-founder, Robert Clivillés, in the wake of the political fracas.
	

	The core issues of the lawsuit are unrelated to what happened with the Trump-related concert pullouts and cancellations. But Clivillés makes it clear in his lawsuit that a contentious, profanity-filled video Williams published on social media in the midst of the controversy was a last straw when it came to pushing him to file suit over rifts that go back three decades or more.


	Clivillés is acting as his own attorney in the suit, which was filed Aug. 14 in the eastern district of New York in United States District Court. He charges Williams with defamation, fraud, trademark infringement, fraud, unfair competition and breach of contract, among other ills, and asks for cancellation of the trademark Williams now holds as well as compensatory and punitive damages adding up to $30 million.


	Clivillés had been warning of his intention to sue Williams for weeks. On Sunday, he posted on social media a video filmed by a process server delivering papers to a figure identified as Williams, who initially keeps walking down the sidewalk as the server drops the paperwork on the ground, before finally agreeing to accept the documents. Williams’ face is not seen in the footage.
	

	The recent video posted by Williams amid the Trump/Freedom 250 controversy comes up for description. “On May 29, 2026,” the suit says, “Williams posted a seven-minute video to the official C+C Music Factory account, which he controls through his fraudulent trademark claim, filmed while sitting on a toilet. In this video… Williams made statements invoking Adolf Hitler, used repeated racial slurs, and directed vulgar and sexually degrading language at members of the public. Plaintiff Clivilles had no warning of and no input into these statements and was forced to launch a competing official C+C Music Factory Instagram account to publicly disavow Williams’ conduct.”

	Clivillés writes that he issued a public legal warning at that time for Williams to stop representing himself with the group name, but rather than back off, Williams allegedly doubled down on June 12 by issuing a new single, “Into the Future,” under the C+C Music Factory name.

	Variety has been unable to reach Clivillés or Williams for comment on the dispute and lawsuit.

	Throughout the suit, Clivillés makes a point in the suit of reaffirming that the letters F or W do not appear in C+C, and that he and the late David Cole (who died in 1995) were the sole members of the outfit, which broke through in 1990 with the No. 1 smash “Gonna Make You Sweat (Everybody Dance Now),” succeeded the following year by the top 10 hits “Here We Go (Let’s Rock & Roll)” and “Things That Make You Go Hmmm…” Williams was listed as a featured artist on all three of those singles, alongside vocalists Martha Wash and Zelma Davis, who also got featured credit. It is Clivillés’ contention that giving Williams and the others featured billing was a way of marking them as guests, as opposed to group members, as is common in pop music. While Clivillés and Cole were primarily producer-writers, he makes the case that they were not unlike famous producers like Quincy Jones who issued albums under their own name while bringing in different singers.

	In Clivillés’ telling, Williams had a production contract with him and Cole, but in mid-1991, around the time “Things That Make You Go Hmmm…” was released, “Williams demanded his release from the 1990 Agreement, stating he did not want to be associated with C+C Music Factory or with Clivillés and Cole’s enterprises going forward. He immediately stopped touring with the group. Sony Music negotiated his release and signed him to a full-length multi-album solo deal. Williams’ first and only solo album fared poorly commercially. C+C Music Factory continued without Williams. Clivillés and Cole released two more albums and several singles” before Cole died in January 1995.
	

	The suit alleges that “beginning in 1996 and continuing to the present, Williams has been performing without authorization under the C+C Music Factory name, obtaining fraudulent trademark registrations in a name that refers to two other people, collecting five thousand to ten thousand dollars per unauthorized show worldwide, and most recently releasing commercial recordings and expanding the unauthorized use of the brand to entirely new parties through Defendant Big Mac Entertainment, LLC.”

	The suit goes on to say that Clivillés and Cole’s estate made a formal estate settlement aggreement that gave Clivillés exclusive use of the C+C Music Factory name. But in 2005, it says, Williams registered “C and C Music Factory” as a trademark, which was canceled in 2012. In 2024, he filed a new trademark application for “C&C Music Factory,” and “as part of his application, Williams affirmed falsely and knowingly that he was the owner of the mark and that no other persons had the right to use the mark in commerce.” Williams was granted the registration in 2015.

	If that’s the case, observers may wonder, why is Clivillés only objecting now? He says he did, in 2016, filing a petition to cancel Williams’ registration. He says it failed to proceed because of a legal error made by his former lawyers, noting that “the proceeding was dismissed with prejudice on June 25, 2018 solely due to Plaintiff’s prior counsel’s failure to file a trial brief. No tribunal has ever adjudicated the substance of Plaintiff’s cancellation claims on the merits.” Clivillés does not explain in the suit whether he ever took any further action after 2018 to try to stop Williams from using the name.

	Clivillés does say he was open to a compromise: “When Plaintiff first became aware that Williams was performing under the C+C Music Factory name, Plaintiff asked WIlliams to bill himself as ‘Freedom Williams formerly of C+C Music Factory. Williams complied briefly before resuming his infringing conduct.”

	In late May, shortly after Morris Day and Young MC gave public notice that they were dropping out of the Trump-approved Freedom 250 concert series, Williams — who had booked the gig under the name C+C Music Factory — posted his angry, attention-getting video about his mixed feelings about whether to stay on the bill or not, indicating that he was leaning toward going ahead. As further artists dropped out and the series fell apart, Williams never did make a subsequent declaration about whether he wanted to go on with the show or not.
	

	Williams said he had been getting upset texts all day and was still catching up. “[N-words] talking about, ‘Yo, Free, you doing the Trump Freedom show?’… I’m like, ‘What are you talking about?’ … Celebrity [n-words] is calling me up, [N-words] I’ve known for years who know I don’t fuck with Trump. … My agent called me about three months ago and said, ‘Yo, you wanna do a show the 25th? In Washington?’” he said today he went back to his agent and said, “‘You didn’t say nothing about Trump. You didn’t mention Trump.’ … So I told my agent, ‘Yeah, no, I ain’t gonna be able to do that.’”

	But then there was a twist in Williams’ thinking, as the eight-minute bathroom rant continued. “I don’t give a fuck about Trump,” he said. “I know the type of fucking anarchy he creates. But the day I let you motherfuckers tell me what to do is the day I die. I want to make that shit motherfucking crystal clear… Listen, I will vote for fucking Genghis Khan, Hitler and motherfucking Ivan the Terrible before I let you [N-words] tell me what to motherfucking do… Y’all can suck my dick with that ‘Don’t do a show for Trump’ shit. I don’t give a fuck about Trump, but I also don’t give a fuck about you either! … Shit, you keep pushing me, I’ll do the motherfucking show in North Korea pissing on a fucking American flag, smoking a Cuban cigar, drinking Venezuelan wine, playing golf with motherfucking Kim Jong-il with an Iranian bitch on my lap while Trump’s standing there with his dick in his hand. That’s how much of a fuck I give what you [n-words] think! You can’t cancel me, pussy, because you don’t exist.” Williams summed up his position by saying, “I might do the motherfucking show,” then ended the video by giving the camera the finger.

title: Shakira, Global Citizen, Live Nation and CAF Commit $1.25 Million to Rebuild Schools in Colombia Following Earthquake
description: Shakira, the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, Live Nation and CAF have announced a $1.25 million initial commitment to rebuild schools following
body:
Shakira, the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, Live Nation and CAF have announced a $1.25 million initial commitment to rebuild schools following the devastating earthquake in Colombia last week. The announcement follows a similar commitment after earthquakes ravaged Venezuela last year.

	Shakira visited Quibdó on Monday alongside philanthropist Howard Buffett and representatives from CAF, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and Fundación Pies Descalzos, following conversations with Global Citizen last week. During the visit she met with Chocó’s Governor, Nubia Carolina Córdoba, and Quibdó’s Mayor, Rafael Bolaños.
	

	In response, an initial commitment of $1.25 million was announced to help rebuild the affected schools. The commitment includes $500,000 from the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, a $500,000 match to the Fund from Live Nation and $250,000 from CAF. Fundación Pies Descalzos will lead the rebuilding efforts in coordination with local authorities and educational communities. The Foundation has worked in Chocó for 22 years.


	Shakira called on the governments of countries including the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada and Japan to join the effort to rebuild the schools affected in Colombia. In Chocó, 40 schools collapsed completely, and 3,207 have been affected across the country.

	Shakira said, “These past few days, I’ve watched my country suffer, but I’ve also watched people come together with the resilience and solidarity that has always defined us. Schools are more than buildings. They give children the stability and routine they need most after a disaster. That’s why we’re making an initial $1.25 million commitment to help rebuild schools and get children back into their classrooms. Chocó is not alone. Colombia is not alone. And we will keep going.”
	

	During the visit, Shakira announced that she will personally dedicate her efforts to the reconstruction of Universidad Tecnológica del Chocó Diego Luis Córdoba, the department’s main public higher education institution, which was also affected by the earthquake.

	“This university is where most of our Pies Descalzos graduates continue their higher education,” she said. “Rebuilding it means protecting the path those young people have already begun.”

	To date, the Howard G Buffett Foundation has invested $340 million since 2008 to fund development programs in Colombia.

	“When disaster strikes, getting children safely back into classrooms is essential to helping communities recover,” said Hugh Evans, Co-Founder and CEO of Global Citizen. “Shakira and Fundación Pies Descalzos have spent decades supporting children in Colombia, and we’re proud that the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund can stand alongside them and the people of Chocó at this moment. This is an initial commitment, and we hope it will encourage others to join the recovery effort.”

	“At CAF, we reaffirm our commitment to Chocó and to all of Colombia in the most difficult moments. Education is the pillar of recovery and sustainable development, which is why we support this joint effort with Shakira, Fundación Pies Descalzos and Global Citizen. Our initial contribution of $250,000 is only the first step of a commitment that must be lasting, because communities are rebuilt through the constant work of all public and private actors. At CAF, we will continue mobilizing resources so that the children of Colombia can safely return to their classrooms,” said Sergio Díaz Granados, CAF’s executive president.

title: American Black Film Festival 2027 Heads to Los Angeles After 24 Years in Miami (EXCLUSIVE)
description: After calling Miami home for the past 24 years, the American Black Film Festival is heading to Los Angeles for its 31st edition, which takes place M
body:
After calling Miami home for the past 24 years, the American Black Film Festival is heading to Los Angeles for its 31st edition, which takes place May 20-23, 2027.

	ABFF 2027 will set up shop across the greater Los Angeles area, making stops at AMC’s Grove location for film screenings and the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures for marquee events. The SLS Hotel in Beverly Hills will serve as the hub for industry programming, and the Original Farmers Market will host activations and community experiences.
	

	“For more than three decades, we’ve built ABFF with the belief that access can change the trajectory of a career and that creating space for new voices strengthens our entire industry,” said Jeff Friday, founder of ABFF and CEO of festival coordinator NICE CROWD. “As we look to the future, our responsibility is to keep pushing forward, expanding what’s possible, and creating greater opportunities for the next generation of storytellers. That’s what this next chapter represents.”


	The 31st edition brings with it new programming, including ABFF First Look: The Studio Showcase, which platforms studios, independent filmmakers and streamers to present upcoming projects. ABFF Sports, which focuses on the intersection of sports, media and entertainment, as well as the noncompetitive film section Crossroads, are likewise coming to ABFF for the first time in 2027.

	“ABFF has always been defined by the people who come together and the sense of community we’ve built over the years,” said Nicole Friday, President of NICE CROWD. “As we look ahead, we want to build on that foundation, creating new opportunities for filmmakers, audiences, industry leaders, and partners to connect while preserving the spirit and sense of belonging that have always made ABFF special.”
	

	Submissions for the 31st ABFF are now open. See the submission categories below.

	U.S. Narrative Feature – A competitive section showcasing feature-length narrative films directed or written by filmmakers of African descent working within the United States. Representing the cornerstone of ABFF’s commitment to discovery, the section highlights distinctive voices, original storytelling, and compelling artistic vision. Selected films compete for the Grand Jury Prize, Directing Award, and Performance Award.

	International Narrative Feature – A competitive section dedicated to feature-length narrative films from across the global Black diaspora. The section celebrates distinctive storytelling voices and cinematic perspectives from outside the United States. Selected films compete for the Grand Jury Prize for International Narrative Feature.

	Documentary Feature – A competitive section presenting feature-length documentaries directed by filmmakers of African descent. The section showcases nonfiction storytelling distinguished by cinematic craft, insight, and cultural relevance. Selected films compete for the Grand Jury Prize for Documentary Feature.

	Crossroads – New Section for 2027 – A non-competitive showcase of narrative and documentary features that explore identity, culture, community, resilience, and belonging through distinctive American experiences. Open to filmmakers of all backgrounds, Crossroads highlights work that aligns with ABFF’s cultural spirit while offering fresh perspectives and meaningful opportunities for connection.

	Episodic Series – A competitive section showcasing episodic storytelling created by filmmakers of African descent. The section highlights compelling serialized narratives and innovative approaches to long-form storytelling. Selected works compete for the Grand Jury Prize for Episodic Series.

	Voices of Culture – Selection by invitation or internal curation only – A non-competitive showcase of short-form work by filmmakers of African descent whose films expand and enrich contemporary conversations around culture, identity, and community. Reflecting the breadth of the global Black experience, the section highlights distinctive voices across genres, forms, and storytelling traditions.

	The ABFF 9:16 Microdrama Project – A non-competitive showcase of original vertical microdrama series created by storytellers of African descent. Dedicated to celebrating emerging creators and new forms of mobile-first storytelling, the section highlights original serialized short-form content from creators working at the forefront of the medium. Selected projects demonstrate strong episodic momentum, emotional immediacy, and a clear command of serialized storytelling.
	

	HBO® Short Film Award – Now in its 30th year, the HBO® Short Film Award remains a cornerstone of ABFF’s commitment to discovering and elevating emerging filmmakers. Each year, five finalists are selected to screen at the festival before a distinguished jury. As an Academy Award-qualifying award, the recipient of the HBO® Short Film Award becomes qualified for consideration in the Live Action Short Film category of the 100th Academy Awards®, subject to all Academy rules and requirements. Submissions for the HBO® Short Film Award will open at a later date, with additional details to be announced.

title: Mother Drowns After Saving 7-Year-Old Son From Illinois River
description:
Illinois Mother
                          Drowns After Rescuing Son From River
body:
Illinois Mother
                          Drowns After Rescuing Son From River
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 18, 2026
                            7:18 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Illinois mother saved her 7-year-old son from a river ... but lost her own life moments after getting him to safety.
      
    
            Angelina Khalimendik was fishing with her three children Sunday evening at Independence Grove Forest Preserve when her youngest son got swept into the Des Plaines River.
      
    
            Officials say Angelina jumped into the water and managed to help her son reach another family member ... but she then went underwater herself.
      

            A relative and nearby bystanders pulled Angelina from the river and attempted CPR before paramedics rushed her to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
      
    
            The coroner said her death was "consistent with drowning."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Police say recent storms made the river deeper and rougher than usual ... with fallen trees, branches, rocks and other debris hidden beneath the surface. Investigators believe the drowning was a tragic accident.
      
    
            Angelina's husband told CBS Chicago he was out of town for work when she took the kids fishing. She leaves behind an 11-year-old daughter and two sons, including a 9-year-old.
      
    
            Angelina was just 31.

Jill Stein
                          Ran For Office ... But Can't Run From the Law!!!

                              August 18, 2026
                            8:22 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jill Stein had a warrant out for her arrest in Missouri after she failed to show up in court for an appearance related to her 2024 assault and trespassing case ... but the warrant has since been dropped.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, the three-time presidential candidate was a no-show in court Monday after she was charged with two misdemeanors -- one count of first-degree trespassing and one count of fourth-degree assault.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The judge issued a warrant -- but it was quickly dropped after her lawyer showed up.
      

            You'll recall ... Jill was arrested during a protest over the Gaza war at Washington University Danforth campus in April 2024 ... and she allegedly kicked a cop several times after grabbing his bicycle while the crowd was being dispersed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jill was the Green Party's presidential nominee in 2012, 2016, and 2024 ... her highest vote total was in '16, when she received more than 1.4 million votes.
      
    
            We've reached out to Jill for comment ... so far, no word back.

title: Rep. Randy Fine Caught Looking Through Homeowner's Mailbox While Campaigning
description:
Rep. Randy Fine
                          CHECKING ALL THE WRONG BOXES
body:
Rep. Randy Fine
                          CHECKING ALL THE WRONG BOXES
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 18, 2026
                            8:58 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Florida Congressman Randy Fine was going door to door looking for votes ... and somehow ended up rifling through a voter's mail.
      
    
            Ring camera footage timestamped Sunday at 4:55 PM ET shows Fine canvassing ahead of Tuesday's Republican primary in Florida's 6th Congressional District ... he's on someone's front porch when he peeks in their mailbox and flips through whatever's inside.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            TMZ has confirmed with Fine's office that it is indeed him in the video.
      
    
            As you can see, Fine rings the doorbell and waits on the porch before he starts looking around. He then lifts the lid of the mailbox and sifts through some envelopes.
      

            Rep. Fine isn't shown removing, tampering with, or inserting anything ... so there's no apparent criminal issue here.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Still ... rifling through a stranger's mailbox is a pretty strange way to win over a voter.
      
    
            Rep. Fine is seeking reelection to the Congressional seat he won last year in a special election.
      
    
            He wants voters checking the box next to his name ... but this weekend, he was the one caught checking a box.

                          Bianca Took My Head Off!!!

            Kanye West is losing his head over his latest music video -- literally -- and wife Bianca Censori is the one calling the shots.
      
    
            Ye dropped the bizarre visual for "OK," his track featuring Don Toliver ... and Bianca planted her husband squarely on a morgue table for the occasion.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            The video shows Kanye as a headless corpse while a team of doctors operates on his body ... pulling strange objects from inside his torso. The medical crew eventually attempts to reattach Ye's head ... turning the whole thing into one seriously twisted resurrection.
      

            Bianca directed the project ... adding another credit to a résumé increasingly filled with her husband's music videos. She previously stepped behind the camera for Ye's visuals for "Father" and "King."
      
    
            "OK" is one of two new tracks added to the deluxe version of Kanye's album "Bully," which was released in June.
      
    
            For Bianca, it seems directing her husband means occasionally taking him apart and putting him back together.
